title: Power budget: what things draw and what sources make
summary: Typical power draw and daily energy use of common loads, what batteries hold, and what solar, pedal, wind, water and fuel can make, with a worked example. Use it to size a battery bank and charging before you haul heavy gear.

steps.text: List every load you want to run.
Find each load's watts: read the label (W), or multiply volts × amps from the label. For DC loads you can measure the current with the meter in series.
Estimate the hours each runs per day. For fridges and freezers, use the daily figure from the table: they cycle on and off.
Multiply watts × hours to get watt-hours (Wh) per day. Add them all up.
Add 20–30% for losses in the inverter, wiring and battery charging.
Battery size in amp-hours = daily Wh × days you must ride through without charging ÷ usable fraction (0.5 for lead-acid, 0.8–0.9 for lithium iron phosphate) ÷ battery volts.
Solar size in watts = daily Wh ÷ (sun hours × 0.75). Use winter sun hours if you need power all year.
Check the biggest single load and its starting surge against your inverter. Motors (fridges, pumps, compressors) can draw 3–7 times their running watts for a moment at start.
If the budget is too big, cut the heat loads first: cooking, water heating and space heating with electricity cost the most. Use fire, gas or the sun for heat.

notes:
All figures are typical ranges. Read the label on the actual device when you can.

## Loads

| Load | Typical draw | Typical use | Energy per day |
|---|---|---|---|
| LED bulb (replaces 60 W) | 7–10 W | 5 h | 35–50 Wh |
| 12 V LED strip | 5–15 W per metre | 5 h | 25–75 Wh per metre |
| Phone, one full charge | 5–20 W while charging | 1 charge | 10–20 Wh |
| Tablet, one full charge | 10–20 W while charging | 1 charge | 25–40 Wh |
| Laptop | 20–60 W | 4 h | 80–240 Wh |
| Wi-Fi router or mesh radio | 6–15 W | 24 h | 150–350 Wh |
| Portable radio receiver | 1–5 W | 4 h | 4–20 Wh |
| CB or ham radio | 5–10 W listening, 20–100 W transmitting | 2 h | 15–50 Wh |
| 12 V compressor fridge (camping or boat type) | 30–60 W running | cycles | 250–600 Wh |
| Home fridge-freezer, modern | 80–150 W running | cycles | 1,000–2,000 Wh (older ones 2,000–4,000) |
| Chest freezer, efficient | 60–100 W running | cycles | 500–1,200 Wh |
| Fan, mains | 30–100 W | 6 h | 180–600 Wh |
| Fan, 12 V | 5–20 W | 6 h | 30–120 Wh |
| LED TV | 30–100 W | 3 h | 90–300 Wh |
| Desktop computer | 60–250 W | 4 h | 240–1,000 Wh |
| CPAP (humidifier off) | 20–60 W | 8 h | 160–480 Wh |
| Home oxygen concentrator | 250–400 W | 24 h | 6,000–9,600 Wh |
| 12 V water pump (diaphragm) | 40–100 W | 1 h | 40–100 Wh |
| Well pump (submersible) | 750–1,500 W running | 1 h | 750–1,500 Wh |
| Washing machine, cold wash | 300–500 W | 1 load | 200–500 Wh per load |
| Microwave oven | 1,000–1,500 W from the wall | 10 min | 170–250 Wh |
| Electric kettle | 1,500–3,000 W | 1 litre boiled | about 100–120 Wh per litre |
| Hot plate or induction ring | 1,000–2,000 W | 1 h | 1,000–2,000 Wh |
| Rice cooker | 300–700 W | 1 batch | 200–400 Wh |
| Slow cooker | 150–300 W | 6–8 h | 1,000–2,000 Wh |
| Electric blanket | 40–100 W | 8 h | 300–800 Wh |
| Space heater | 1,000–2,000 W | 4 h | 4,000–8,000 Wh |
| Corded power tools | 500–1,500 W | 15 min | 125–375 Wh |
| Inverter left on with no load | 5–50 W | 24 h | 120–1,200 Wh |

Heat is expensive. Anything that heats with electricity (kettles, heaters, cookers, hair dryers) eats a small system in minutes.

## Storage

| Battery | Nominal energy | Usable for long life |
|---|---|---|
| Phone battery | 10–20 Wh | most of it |
| 18650 cell | 7–12 Wh | about 80% |
| Power tool pack (18–20 V) | 35–100 Wh | about 80% |
| Laptop pack | 40–100 Wh | about 80% |
| UPS battery, 12 V 7–9 Ah | 85–110 Wh | about 50% |
| E-bike pack | 300–750 Wh | about 80% |
| Car starting battery, 12 V 45–70 Ah | 540–840 Wh | 20–30%: not built for deep use |
| Deep-cycle lead-acid, 12 V 100 Ah | 1,200 Wh | about 600 Wh (50%) |
| Golf-cart or scrubber battery, 6 V 200–230 Ah | 1,200–1,400 Wh | about 600–700 Wh |
| Lithium iron phosphate, 12.8 V 100 Ah | 1,280 Wh | about 1,000–1,150 Wh |
| Electric car pack | 40–100 kWh | specialist work only: lethal voltage |

Energy (Wh) = volts × amp-hours.

## Sources

| Source | Output | Per day |
|---|---|---|
| 100 W solar panel | up to about 75 W in full sun | about 300–500 Wh in summer, 100–250 Wh in winter or cloud |
| Pedal generator, fit adult | 50–100 W steady | 50–100 Wh per hour of pedalling |
| Hand crank | 5–20 W | small top-ups only |
| Small wind turbine, rated 400 W | rarely near rated | often 200–1,000 Wh at a good windy site; far less in sheltered spots |
| Micro-hydro, 100 W | steady day and night | about 2,400 Wh: the best source if you have a stream with a drop |
| Car idling with alternator and inverter | 300–1,000 W usable | burns about 0.5–1.5 litres of fuel an hour |
| Portable petrol generator, 1–3 kW | up to its rating | burns about 0.4–1.2 litres an hour depending on load |

Sun hours: the number of hours of full-strength sun a day is about 4–7 in summer in sunny places and as low as 1–2 in winter far from the equator. Generators and idling engines make carbon monoxide: run them outdoors, away from windows and doors.

## Worked example: a small cabin

| Load | Calculation | Wh per day |
|---|---|---|
| 4 LED lights | 4 × 8 W × 5 h | 160 |
| 2 phones | 2 × 15 Wh | 30 |
| Radio | 3 W × 4 h | 12 |
| Laptop | 40 W × 3 h | 120 |
| 12 V fridge | from table | 400 |
| Total | | 722 |
| Plus 25% losses | | about 900 |

Battery for 2 days without sun, lead-acid at 50% usable, 12 V: 900 × 2 ÷ 0.5 ÷ 12 = 300 Ah, three 100 Ah batteries. With lithium iron phosphate at 85%: about 180 Ah.

Solar with 4 sun hours: 900 ÷ (4 × 0.75) = 300 W of panels.
